Subject: Request: separation evidence for Bridgewater deployment

Marcus —

Thanks for the demo last week. As part of our vendor security intake we need a concise evidence packet covering how Redwood isolates Bridgewater workloads from other tenants and from the control plane. Can you provide the following by COB Thu (2026-10-07)?

- A network-level diagram showing VPCs/subnets, sidecar placement, load-balancer/egress paths, and any cross-tenant interconnects.
- A short written description of the isolation model (tenant carve-up, shared control plane specifics, where KV cache lives).
- Threat summary: top 3 attack paths you consider highest-risk for multi-tenant inference and the mitigations in place.
- Sample flow logs (anonymized) demonstrating egress restrictions for a sample tenant.
- Any signed attestations or evidence bundles you can share (SOC references, audit checklist items).

If some items are sensitive, a redacted version is fine. We can set up a call to walk a security engineer through the diagrams and logs.

Appreciate the quick turnaround — Bridgewater is aiming for approval ahead of the next procurement window.

Regards,
Alice Mueller
Head of Vendor Security
Bridgewater Financial

Alice — thanks for the clear checklist. We've pulled together an evidence packet and I attached an initial diagram and appendix. High-level notes below; full items are in the attachments and in the Drive link I'm adding to related_links.

Summary (high level):
- Isolation model: Customers are logically separated via per-tenant VPCs at the orchestration layer. The control plane is a Redacted-managed control plane in a separate VPC and communicates over mutual-TLS to customer-side connectors. Model runtime workers are pinned to tenancy pools; we use a sidecar per-pod for egress policy and auth enforcement. KV cache lives as an encrypted, per-tenant cache instance colocated with the runtime pool (not in the shared control plane).
- Network topology (see network_separation_diagram_v3.svg): public ingress terminates at a regional LB in a dedicated edge VPC. From there requests route to tenant-isolated runtime pools (private subnets) through an internal routing fabric.
- Egress & guardrails: egress is restricted by per-tenant allowlists and enforced at the sidecar and regional egress gateways. We publish a per-tenant egress policy, and there is an automated circuit-breaker that routes to a lower-capacity fallback model variant if a region/burst causes cross-tenant routing pressure.
- Threat summary (top 3):
  1) Cross-tenant data leakage via shared kernel/unsafe serialization — mitigation: strict process-level sandboxing, per-tenant cache separation, and automated canaries that detect anomalous KV access patterns.
  2) Lateral movement through compromised operator credentials — mitigation: short-lived operator session tokens, strong control-plane RBAC, and mandatory approval workflows for cross-tenant configuration changes.
  3) Egress exfiltration via indirect prompt-chaining / function calls — mitigation: function calling is sandboxed, outgoing requests from models must pass through egress policy enforcement and are logged to immutable storage for 90 days (configurable).

Attachments included in this email (zipped where appropriate):
- network_separation_diagram_v3.svg (diagram; annotated)
- isolation_threat_appendix_v1.pdf (threat model + mitigation mapping)
- flow-sample-20261005.csv (anonymized flow log sample)

Next steps: if that looks good, we can schedule a 30-minute walkthrough with our infra and security engineers (Irene will be the architecture lead on the call). Vanessa — can you validate whether we should include a short signed attestation or the full SOC reference bundle for Bridgewater?

Thanks,

Marcus Lin
Senior Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

Thanks Marcus — packet looks good. Two quick asks before we share the bundle externally:

1) Add a short section (<= 300 words) that explains KV-cache lifecycle and key material handling. Bridgewater's team asked specifically about cache residency during model warmup and ghost-cache scenarios. Keep it non-sensitive — high-level controls only.
2) Include our attestation (one-page) rather than the full SOC bundle. Procurement prefers a concise signed attestation for initial approval; keep the SOC references as a link in the appendix.

Irene — can you confirm that the sample flow logs contain no tenant-identifying metadata? If they do, redact and resubmit.

Marcus — if you can fold the two items into the evidence bundle, I'll approve for outbound to Bridgewater. Also label the Drive folder with the Bridgewater NDA tag so Legal can track access.

Vanessa Ortiz
